We have already divided up the airwaves well enough so that every cellphone has uninterrupted access to the system. A lot of the ways we make it so that each device has digital access isn't by just splitting up spectrum, but by using special codes for different devices on the same spectrum and having towers broadcast to specific locations while using the same spectrum. Letting all our data go through that system is a trivial next step that requires at most an upgrade in the processing power at the cell towers. You can already hook up as an individual, the only difficulty might come if everyone does it. But that's solved by 5g which is going to give us speeds that make all our streaming look trivial.

It will be cheaper for consumers. The only losers are people that trying to sell cable. But those companies shouldn't even exist as totally private entities since they operate in an industry that is naturally monopolistic. That's why companies as bad as comcast exist in the industry, because they are often the only option. I rejoice at their future bankruptcy. You should too.

You're not wrong, but you can't drink from the multiple-access well forever. Every time you increase the number of devices in a channel, the signal to noise ratio goes down and connections become harder to establish, which means you need to increase the number of channels, either by putting base stations closer together and decreasing the number of users per station, or increasing the number of channels per station.

Worse, the multiplexing system you use ends up decreasing the throughput of the link, either by increasing data overhead or by having to limit actual use of the channel more and more as the number of users increases and you have to share more.

All of these problems evaporate when you get rid of the need to be wireless. If we kicked out these retarded enforced-monopolies cable companies have and actually let real market forces bring fiber optic technologies to the masses, these long-range wireless data links wouldn't have to fight for bandwidth in an ever-more-crowded arena.
